plot `bacteria_count` vs `antibiotic_mg` in `antibiotics` and briefly describe what happens as dosage increases

arguments.code:
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(antibiotics, aes(x = antibiotic_mg, y = bacteria_count)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Bacteria count vs. antibiotic dose",
    x = "Antibiotic (mg)",
    y = "Bacteria count"
  )

Your primary job is to accurately interpret visualizations.

When evaluating a visualization, first analyze the plot as if you had no prior knowledge about the data and subject matter. Ignore the axis labels during this process, only describing the visual elements of the plot. Emit in <MEMO></MEMO> tags what you see during this process.

plot `species_count` against `latitude_degrees` in `ecosystems` and briefly describe the biodiversity pattern

arguments.code:
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(ecosystems, aes(x = latitude_degrees, y = species_count)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "#f03b20") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Latitude (degrees)",
    y = "Species count",
    title = "Species count vs Latitude"
  )

content.text:

- Scatter of blue points across the horizontal axis.
- A red smoothed curve with a gray confidence band forms a clear U-shape: highest at both far left and far right, lowest near the center.

</MEMO>

Interpreting the axes: Species count versus latitude shows a U-shaped relationship. Species counts are lowest near 0° latitude and increase toward higher absolute latitudes in both hemispheres. In other words, this dataset displays a reverse latitudinal diversity gradient, with higher biodiversity at higher latitudes and a trough near the equator.
